Ok. Imagine photons as classical particles that follow a corkscrew trajectory

If you try to model a photon as a classical particle with a corkscrew (helical) trajectory, the first immediate question is: corkscrew in what sense—space, spacetime, or just in some internal coordinate?

If it’s literal spatial motion (a particle moving forward while spiraling), that already breaks the simplest constraint: a photon in vacuum has no rest frame and must move at invariant speed \(c\) along a null worldline. A true spatial helix implies transverse acceleration and therefore changing momentum direction, which would normally require a force and would also introduce a well-defined rest frame in the transverse plane. That clashes with Lorentz invariance for a massless particle.

If instead you mean a helical *worldline* in spacetime, you run into a different issue: null curves in Minkowski space don’t support “spiraling” in the usual Euclidean sense. You can parameterize complicated null trajectories, but any structure that looks like periodic transverse motion typically implies either superluminal components in some frame or an effective mass term.

Where the idea *does* connect to something real is polarization. A circularly polarized photon has a field whose electric vector rotates as it propagates. That can look superficially like “corkscrewing,” but crucially the rotation is not the particle’s path—it’s the internal phase of the electromagnetic field. The photon still travels straight; what rotates is the field orientation in the transverse plane.

There’s also a more speculative bridge people sometimes reach for: internal “zitterbewegung”-like pictures or de Broglie-style internal clocks, where a particle has some kind of rapid internal rotation at Compton-scale frequencies. But for photons (massless), even that construction becomes slippery because there’s no rest frame in which to define an internal oscillation in the usual way.

So the short version is: a corkscrew trajectory works nicely as an image for rotating phase or helicity, but as literal classical motion through space it conflicts with the geometry of null propagation and Lorentz invariance.

If you want, we can try to formalize your idea in a way that *does* survive relativity—e.g., by encoding the corkscrew as a constraint on a null worldline bundle, or as a geometric phase in a fiber-bundle picture of electromagnetism.

If you try to force photons into a classical particle picture, a “corkscrew trajectory” is actually one of the more natural-seeming intuitions people land on—but it runs into a hard mismatch with what the physics is really tracking.

What you’re probably gesturing toward is something like: “as it moves forward, the photon also has some internal rotational motion,” so the path in space becomes helical. That picture *does* resemble a few real ideas—but none of them are literal trajectories in space.

In classical electromagnetism, light is not a point particle following a path at all. It’s an oscillating electromagnetic field. The closest real analog of your corkscrew intuition shows up in polarization. For circularly polarized light, the electric field vector rotates in a plane perpendicular to propagation, tracing a helix in *field space* rather than in physical space. The wave moves forward in a straight line; what “corkscrews” is the field orientation, not the energy packet’s path.

In quantum electrodynamics, photons are excitations of that field. They don’t have a well-defined trajectory between emission and detection in the classical sense. What you can assign is momentum, energy, and helicity (spin angular momentum aligned or anti-aligned with motion). That helicity is sometimes informally visualized as “twist,” which is probably what your corkscrew idea is trying to capture.

If you literally impose a spatial helix on a photon’s path, you immediately break Lorentz invariance in a visible way: different inertial frames would disagree about the geometry of the path in a way that the Maxwell/QED description avoids. Also, you’d lose the experimentally verified straight-line propagation in vacuum (up to interactions/gravity).

So the clean mapping is:

- Corkscrew *trajectory in space* → not supported experimentally
- Corkscrew *rotation of field phase / polarization* → real (circular/elliptical polarization)
- Corkscrew *as particle spin intuition* → metaphor for helicity, not motion

If you want, we can push this idea further in a more disciplined way: you can actually build a quasi-classical model where photons are wavepackets with center-of-energy motion straight, while the internal phase rotates like a helical fiber bundle. That’s much closer to how modern field theory encodes “twist” without giving up relativity.
I didn’t ask for a critique. I asked you to imagine it

Okay—taking it as a pure construct.

A photon is a classical point-like particle moving through vacuum, but instead of traveling in a straight line, it follows a perfectly uniform corkscrew trajectory.

The axis of the corkscrew is the net direction of propagation. Along that axis, the photon advances at constant speed \(c\). Superimposed on this forward motion is a perpendicular circular motion with constant radius. So in space it traces a helix: forward drift + transverse rotation.

From the photon’s own “motion law,” nothing accelerates in the usual sense. The curvature is intrinsic, not caused by external forces. At every instant, its velocity vector is tangent to the helix and always has magnitude \(c\). The direction of motion continuously rotates, but speed never changes.

A full cycle of the corkscrew corresponds to a fixed intrinsic scale: one wavelength. So after traveling one wavelength along the axis, the photon has completed exactly one full rotation around it and returns to the same transverse phase position.

Different photons differ in the handedness of the corkscrew. Right-handed helices correspond to one internal “spin orientation,” left-handed to the opposite. Linear polarization becomes the degenerate case where two opposite helices are superposed, producing a wobbling or ribbon-like trajectory that oscillates back and forth rather than forming a clean spiral.

A beam of such photons looks like a bundle of tightly aligned helices, like a braided rope of light. Coherent laser light is a perfectly ordered braid; incoherent light is a tangled field of overlapping corkscrews with drifting phases, making the structure statistically invisible.

Interactions occur when helices intersect matter: absorption happens when the corkscrew phase matches an allowed rotational state of the target, while scattering corresponds to a partial deflection of the helix axis with the internal rotation preserved.

In this model, “color” is literally the pitch of the corkscrew: higher frequency means tighter, faster axial rotation—more coils per unit distance.

So the photon is not a straight dart of energy. It is a rigid, self-propagating helix, translating forward while eternally spinning around its own path.
What does it do to thr double slit experiment

In your corkscrew-photon picture, the double-slit experiment becomes a very geometric interference problem about how helices pass through two openings and later “re-sum” in space.

Start with a single photon: a rigid helix advancing toward a barrier with two slits.

At the slit plane, the helix is effectively “sampled” by the aperture. What matters is not a point passing through one slit, but which portion of the corkscrew phase is aligned with each opening. So each slit doesn’t just transmit “a particle”—it transmits a *slice of the helix’s phase structure*.

After the barrier, there are now two allowed helical continuations:

- one helix emerging from slit A  
- one helix emerging from slit B  

Both continue forward with the same intrinsic corkscrew structure, but now they are spatially offset and slightly out of phase depending on path length differences.

As these two helical trajectories propagate, their transverse circular motions interfere in space. Not as fields, in this model, but as overlapping geometric paths of rotating particles.

So the key feature becomes this:

At any detection screen point, the photon is not arriving via a single trajectory but via the *superposition of two possible helix segments*, and what matters is whether their rotational phases align or cancel when they arrive at the same location.

Constructively interfering regions are where the corkscrew phase from slit A and slit B land in the same transverse orientation at the same time. There, the helix “reinforces” occupancy probability and detection is likely.

Destructive regions are where one helix arrives rotated half a cycle relative to the other. In your geometry, that means the transverse motion is always misaligned at that point, so the particle effectively never “lands coherently” there.

So the screen ends up with bands corresponding to stable phase-locking between two spatially separated corkscrew streams.

A useful way to phrase the outcome in this model:

The interference pattern is not caused by wave addition in space, but by *phase synchronization between two competing helical paths projected onto the same detection surface*.

And a single photon still produces one dot per run—but each dot is sampled from a distribution shaped by where those helical phase alignments are stable.
So. It deserves the double slit
So. It preserves the double slit. Does it look anything like Bohmian paths

Yes—within your corkscrew-particle picture, it naturally “earns” a double-slit-style pattern.

But the important point is what actually carries the structure. It’s not the particle splitting or choosing a path in the usual sense. It’s that the helix has an internal phase that keeps evolving, and the two slits act like two spatially separated samplers of that same evolving phase.

So the pattern comes from this:

- the corkscrew continues with a well-defined internal rotation
- each slit re-launches a copy of that phase-aligned structure from

Yes—there’s a real resemblance in *structure*, but also a clean difference in what’s doing the work.

Your corkscrew photon picture produces something visually and conceptually close to Bohmian trajectories in one specific sense: it restores a single, continuous path for each particle, and the interference pattern emerges from how that path is guided by a global constraint.

In Bohmian mechanics, the particle has a definite position at all times, but its velocity is guided by the wavefunction’s phase field. So the “weirdness” lives in a nonlocal guiding equation rather than in the particle’s motion itself. The trajectories can look smooth, curving, sometimes looping through regions in ways that mimic “flow lines” of a wave.

In your model, the photon is also a single continuous object with a definite path—but the “guidance” is internalized differently. Instead of an external pilot wave, the structure of the path itself already contains the phase information: the corkscrew encodes what Bohmian mechanics would distribute into a separate wavefield.

So the mapping looks like this:

- Bohm: straight-ish particle + external wavefunction field that bends its velocity
- Corkscrew photon: no external field doing guidance; the geometry of motion *already contains the phase evolution*

Where they start to diverge sharply is this:

In Bohmian mechanics, two nearby trajectories can diverge because the guiding wave depends on the entire experimental setup (nonlocal dependence on boundary conditions).

In the corkscrew model, the path is locally rigid: it doesn’t get “steered” by distant slit geometry. Instead, the slit structure would have to act by selecting or phase-slicing portions of the helix, and the interference pattern emerges downstream from how those slices re-align.

So Bohmian paths are like flowlines in a river whose current field changes depending on the whole riverbed.

Corkscrew paths are like rigid screws passing through gates that filter their phase, and the pattern comes from recombination rather than continuous steering.

Visually, though, if you plotted many runs, both models give you something very similar: smooth, continuous trajectories that statistically reproduce the same interference fringes.

The deep difference is ontological:

- Bohm: trajectory is *passive*, wave is primary
- Corkscrew: trajectory is *self-contained*, wave-like behavior is encoded in motion itself

If you pushed your model hard enough, you’d basically be reinventing a kind of “geometric Bohmian mechanics,” except with helicity baked into kinematics rather than emerging from a separate guiding field.
